planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil, spacing plants generously to accommodate Cabot's vigorous, spreading growth habit.

directions: Cabot was released in 1998 from the Kentville research station in Nova Scotia and is grown for its unusually large, pale-red, glossy berries produced over a mid-season harvest window. Plants carry relatively few blossoms per crown but compensate with fruit size, and the cultivar shows good resistance to red stele root rot, a soilborne disease common in cool, humid strawberry ground. Its cold hardiness and vigor have made it popular with home growers throughout the Canadian Maritimes and the New England states. Thin runners regularly to keep berry size from declining as matted rows fill in.

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; mulch over winter in the coldest parts of its range.

directions: Glooscap is a 1983 release from the Kentville breeding program in Nova Scotia, bred from a cross of Micmac and Bounty, and remains valued decades later for its exceptional winter hardiness and heavy mid-season yields. The medium-sized berries separate cleanly from the cap at harvest, a trait that makes hulling for jam and preserves noticeably faster than with many dessert-type cultivars. Its toughness has made it a long-standing recommendation for cold-climate gardens from Newfoundland to the northern Plains. Renovate beds after harvest by mowing foliage and thinning runners to sustain productivity in following years.

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Annapolis roots quickly and produces abundant runners for filling matted rows.

directions: Annapolis was bred at the Kentville research station in Nova Scotia and released in 1984 as an Earliglow-derived selection resistant to red stele root rot, giving northern growers an early cultivar for sites with a history of root disease. Fruit is medium-large, light red, and mildly sweet, ripening ahead of most other hardy June-bearers and extending the start of the home harvest season. The vigorous, freely runnering plants tolerate winters to zone 3 with only modest straw mulch protection. Because it fruits early, protect open blossoms from late spring frosts with row cover when a cold snap is forecast.

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; a heavy straw mulch over winter is important in the coldest parts of its range.

directions: Veestar is an Ontario-bred June-bearer prized across the Canadian prairies and northern U.S. Midwest for combining very early ripening with exceptional winter hardiness. The first flush of berries is notably large and firm with bright red color and good flavor, though fruit size drops off quickly as the harvest continues, so the earliest picks give the best quality. Its vigor and productivity have kept it a standard recommendation for short-season, cold-winter gardens for decades. Apply a thick winter mulch and remove it gradually in spring to protect crowns from late freezes without delaying growth.
sources: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained, disease-free soil, spacing to allow good air movement around the freely runnering plants.

directions: Redchief was released in 1968 by the USDA Beltsville station working with the Maryland Agricultural Experiment Station and became an important early-midseason cultivar for growers battling red stele root rot, resisting several known races of the pathogen. It also carries moderate resistance to verticillium wilt, leaf scorch, and powdery mildew, giving it broader disease tolerance than many older cultivars of its era. Berries are medium-large, sweet, and attractive, produced on vigorous plants that runner freely to fill in rows. Rotate planting sites and avoid old strawberry ground even with resistant cultivars like Redchief to limit buildup of other soilborne problems.

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil, and cover with straw mulch before the ground freezes to protect crowns through severe winters.

directions: Cyclone is a June-bearing strawberry noted for reliable survival to zone 3, making it a long-time favorite for home gardens across Minnesota, the Dakotas, and other regions with severe winters. Its concentrated harvest window is short compared to many cultivars, typically lasting about ten days, so plan for prompt picking and processing once the medium-to-large, bright red berries begin to ripen. Flavor is sweet and full-bodied, suiting fresh eating as well as freezing and preserving. Because the bulk of the crop ripens quickly, staggering plantings of an earlier and later cultivar alongside Cyclone can extend the overall harvest season.
